domain: High-Reliability Organizations / Safety Training / Competence Maintenance
topic_summary: Analysis of catastrophe-avoidance competence retention in aviation (stall recovery, crew resource management) and nuclear sectors (meltdown-avoidance), examining whether simulation-based training constitutes sufficient exercise to maintain competence over decades without recurring real catastrophes, or whether only actual catastrophic incidents can occupy the competence kernel.

key_entities: FAA (regulatory mandate-setter for aviation training requirements)
ICATEE (International Committee for Aviation Training in Extended Envelopes, formed 2009)
Airlines and flight training organizations (competence delivery agents)
key_tensions: Simulation as proxy-catastrophe vs simulation as insufficient substitute (core kernel contest)
Demonstrated competence under jeopardy conditions vs actual practice in non-jeopardy operations
Skill decay timeline (6-12 months) vs training refresh intervals (1-2 years desired, actual varies)
High-fidelity environmental realism vs missing human factors elements in simulation
key_mechanisms: Low-dose high-frequency (LDHF) training to prevent skill deterioration
Booster training when competency begins to wane
Line audits under non-jeopardy conditions to assess real operational behavior
key_absences: Consensus on optimal timing and intensity for maintenance training
Validated metrics for measuring real-world competence transfer from simulation

commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory bodies (FAA, nuclear regulators) mandate training requirements; professional consensus and post-incident investigations ground interpretive legitimacy

readings.expected_structural_delta: Training compliance becomes the observable; skill decay treated as solvable via frequency/fidelity optimization; simulation industry becomes primary beneficiary

readings.commitment: Only actual catastrophic incidents provide the authentic conditions necessary to occupy the competence kernel
readings.authority_grounding: Empirical observation of jeopardy paradox (assessed performance ≠ actual practice), skill decay despite simulation, missing human factors
readings.expected_structural_delta: Rare real incidents become the observable; high-reliability organizations face unresolvable competence maintenance problem; no viable beneficiary structure (catastrophes are unacceptable)

readings.commitment: Competence occupation requires continuous multi-mechanism exercise (simulation + refresher + procedural reinforcement + line audits) without consensus on optimal configuration
readings.authority_grounding: Systematic review evidence of skill decay timelines, LDHF/booster training literature, line audit findings
readings.expected_structural_delta: Multiple observables (simulation performance, line audit behavior, skill decay curves); no single mechanism sufficient; training optimization becomes perpetual research problem

axiom_contradictions.basis: Simulation_sufficiency axiom holds that controlled replication of catastrophic conditions is structurally equivalent to the real event for competence maintenance. Real_incident_necessity axiom holds that authentic jeopardy conditions (uncontrolled, genuine consequences) are structurally irreplaceable. No single framework can hold both: either simulation is proxy-catastrophe (making real incidents unnecessary) or it is not (making them necessary). The jeopardy paradox evidence suggests the axioms are mutually exclusive.

omegas.description: Does hybrid_occupation reading collapse into 'we don't know the optimal mix' rather than a distinct structural constraint? If so, the kernel contest reduces to simulation_sufficiency vs real_incident_necessity binary, with skill_decay_despite_simulation as the unresolved empirical challenge to sufficiency.
omegas.source: Kernel/reading decomposition (§1.3-K); hybrid_occupation deferred as scaffold

omegas.description: Absence of consensus on optimal timing/intensity for maintenance training suggests the competence occupation kernel may be fundamentally unstable—no configuration reliably prevents decay. If true, high-reliability organizations face structural impossibility: rare catastrophes cannot be allowed to occur (for competence maintenance) but simulation cannot prevent skill decay.
omegas.source: Absence inventory (§1.1); systematic review evidence of overlapping terminology without consensus

omegas.description: Missing validated metrics for measuring real-world competence transfer from simulation. Line audit data suggests jeopardy paradox (assessed ≠ actual), but no consensus observable exists to measure whether simulation-acquired competence transfers to authentic catastrophe response. This measurement gap may be structural rather than methodological.
omegas.source: Absence inventory (§1.1); line audit findings vs simulation assessment gap

omegas.description: Is real_incident_necessity a true mountain (physics of authentic jeopardy conditions) or a piton of current measurement limitations? If validated transfer metrics existed, simulation_sufficiency might be empirically testable rather than axiomatically contested.
omegas.source: F03 (Hasty Generalization); mountain classification for real_incident_necessity based on jeopardy paradox evidence

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: real_incident_necessity classified as mountain based on jeopardy paradox evidence and missing human factors in simulation, but this may reflect current measurement limitations rather than irreducible physics of authentic jeopardy. If validated transfer metrics existed, the mountain/rope distinction might collapse. Generated omega_mountain_validity to bound this uncertainty. Kernel contest is genuine: simulation_sufficiency and real_incident_necessity hold mutually exclusive axioms about whether controlled replication equals authentic conditions for competence maintenance.
